title: Why Contracts?
concept: Contracts are explicit promises a function makes about its inputs and outputs, enforced by the compiler and runtime.
why: Without contracts, bugs like division by zero, null pointer dereference, and out-of-bounds access cause silent corruption or crashes far from the root cause.
tips: Contracts move bug detection from the crash site to the violation site
Think of `requires` as "what the caller owes me" and `ensures` as "what I owe the caller"
Contracts serve as live documentation — always up-to-date because they're enforced
Design by Contract was pioneered by Bertrand Meyer in Eiffel
common_mistakes: Putting business logic inside requires — contracts should only validate, not compute
Writing contracts that can't be checked at compile time without realising it
Forgetting that contracts are stripped in release builds unless --runtime-contracts is set
